summary: A satirical piece about low voter turnout in Smalltown on Election Day, September 17th, 2023. It describes failed attempts to lure voters, including hot dog stands, glow-in-the-dark stickers, the 'Swipe to Vote' app, a historical reenactment, door-to-door canvassing, a student campaign, and a dance-off. It ends by noting that apathy persists and democracy 'waits for everyone'.
one_line: A humorous satire of Smalltown's failed schemes to boost voter turnout on Election Day, September 17th, 2023.
key_facts: Election Day in Smalltown was September 17th, 2023, and turnout was very low.
Local politician Bob "Ballot" Barker joked, "If only we had as many voters as we do potholes, we'd be the envy of democracies worldwide!"
The municipality offered hot dog stands (free with proof of voting) and glow-in-the-dark "I Voted" stickers, but the results were lackluster.
Smalltown introduced a voting app called 'Swipe to Vote' with customizable avatars, but excitement faded because there were no rewards or badges for 'Super Voter' status.
Local influencer Clara Clickbait complained she could not share her voting streak or get social cred.
The Council reenacted the 'Battle for Ballots' from 1789, and Councilman Joe "Just Vote" Jefferson wore a tricorner hat and declared "No taxation without representation!"
The reenactment drew a crowd of children with popcorn, and the audience asked if there was a gun salute for early voters.

Dorothy "Doorbell" Dawkins went door-to-door to rouse voters; residents peeked through curtains or said "We're just visiting" or "I thought it was tomorrow", and pamphlets were used as coasters or fly swatters.
The 'Vote or Bust' college campaign used the slogan "Your voice, your vote, your very ambiguous future!", but students lingered outside the polling station as if it were a latte spot.
Student Chad "Chill" Chalmers said he had class during voting hours and asked for an "absentee latte, I mean, ballot".
Mayor Beatrice "Boogie" Banks hosted the "Ballot Boogie", a dance-off where a vote was the ticket to the floor.
Rico "Rhythm" Rodriguez, a candidate for public works, became notorious for his salsa sequence rather than his policies.
The day ended with deserted polling booths and the conclusion that rhythm did not translate into political engagement.
